Financial repercussions of data breaches

What are the sources (direct/indirect) of costs related to data breaches?

Direct (money paid out)

  • Legal (fees, fines/penalties, settlements)
  • Incident response (outside forensic experts, crisis management)
  • Notification (letters/emails to customers, reporting to regulators)
  • Customer support (outsourced hotline for complaints)
  • Victim remediation (credit monitoring, new cards/accounts)
  • PR agency to “repair” the brand
  • Ransom payment (if paid)

Indirect (lost value & internal effort)

  • Business disruption (downtime → lost revenue; IT staff time)
  • Lost customers and fewer new customers
  • Reputational damage (diminished goodwill)
  • Staff time and management distraction
  • Increased insurance premiums, higher borrowing costs
  • Follow-on IT/security investments (update/harden systems; not counted by IBM)

→ Public companies: market response (decrease in stock price)

    Attackers and their motivation

    The players

    Hackers* – someone who breaks into computer systems

    White hat hackers

    • Uncover computer weaknesses without exploiting them.
    • Contribute to improving system security.

    Black hat hackers

    • Computer criminals who exploit a system’s weakness for personal gain (can be state or company sponsored).

    Hacktivists

    Target firms, web sites, or even users as a protest measure (e.g., Anonymous).

    or press →

    *The term hacker is sometimes also referred to a particularly skilled/clever programmer

    INSY 2299 · Session 13
    Attackers and their motivation

    Hackers’ motivation varies

    • $$$
    • Cyberwarfare
    • Terrorism
    • Corporate espionage (including intellectual property theft)
    • Extortionists
    • Revenge (disgruntled employees)
    • Protest hacking (“hacktivism”)
    • Pranksters

    In most cases the incentives largely boil down to:

    Attacker ROI=Asset value to attacker – Cost of attackCost of the attack

    ROI: Return on investment

    or press →. The next slide puts numbers on it.

    Often cited: 69% of hackers are motivated purely by financial considerations, e.g., account theft and illegal funds transfer; some data harvesters sell their take to cash-out fraudsters, who buy (then resell) goods with stolen cards or open false accounts via identity theft. Original report not identified.

    Common types of attacks

    Leading threats/attack types

    Virus

    Programs that infect other software or files and require an executable and the user to spread.

    Worm

    Virus type/software that replicates itself by taking advantage of security vulnerability to spread across network connections (to other devices).

    Trojans

    Attempt to sneak in by masquerading as something they’re not.

    NotesA virus attaches itself to a program, file, or disk and activates when it is executed. Recover/prevent: avoid unreliable websites/emails, System Restore, re-install the OS, anti-virus (e.g., Avira, AVG, Norton).
    ⬇

    Malware

    Umbrella term for malicious software that seek to compromise a computing system without permission.

    INSY 2299 · Session 13
    Common types of attacks

    Potential consequences of malware

    Botnets

    Zombie computers (networks of infiltrated and compromised clients controlled by a central command) that are used for all sorts of crimes.

    Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)

    Effectively shutting down Web sites by overwhelming them with a crushing load of seemingly legitimate requests sent simultaneously by thousands of clients.

    Many large organizations have been victims of such attacks (e.g., Amazon, Yahoo, Microsoft, The White House)

    Ransomware attack

    Blocking access to systems/files/data by the means of encryption unless ransom is paid. Sometimes combined with the threat to publish the data. Type of attack is on the rise partly due to the popularity of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies (which make payments harder to trace).

        Encryption

        Scrambling data using a code, thereby hiding it from those who do not have the unlocking key

        Key

        Code that unlocks encryption.

        Public key encryption

        Two key system used for securing electronic transmissions.

        Certificate authority

        Trusted third party that provides authentication services in public key encryption schemes

        Message
        3
        Ciphertext
        3
        Decrypted

        Both sides need the same key, so it has to be shared first, somehow, without anyone listening.

        Bank’s public keypublished to everyone
        (e = 17, n = 3233)
        Bank’s private keynever leaves the bank
        (d = 2753, n = 3233)
        Ciphertext
        Decrypted

        Anyone can lock with the public key; only the private key unlocks. A certificate authority vouches that the public key really is the bank’s (the browser padlock). Toy numbers: real keys are 2048+ bits.

        What might hold (small and medium sized) companies back from investing in information security?

        Class answers

          INSY 2299 · Session 13
          Information security

          Conclusion

          Information security breaches are on the rise and have tremendous consequences: aggravated by the increasing digitization and connectivity (e.g., email, websites, mobile devices as well as internet of things) of business processes (e.g., banking, ecommerce/payment, etc.), and by more capable AI tools, allowing less technical actors to enter the scene.

          Information security must be made a top organizational priority (regulation can align incentives!)

          Zero trust

          Never trust, always verify. Assume attacker is already inside a system. Continuous authentication & micro-segmentation.

          AI cyber defense

          Fight AI with AI: spot anomalies and phishing at machine speed, triage alerts, automate response. Extensive users cut breach costs by $1.9M and contained breaches 80 days faster.*

          Patch management

          Inventory all software and update fast. With ~48,000 new vulnerabilities in 2025 (slide 8), prioritize those actually exploited (e.g., CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list) and automate rollout.

          or press →

          *IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025: organizations using security AI and automation extensively vs. organizations not using them (average breach cost USD 3.62M vs. 5.52M).

          INSY 2299 · Session 13
          Appendix · AI-enabled attacks

          ARTEX: an AI pen-testing framework turned attack tool

          • What it is: an open-source, AI-driven penetration-testing framework posted on GitHub in mid-2026. Six specialized AI sub-agents split up the attack: reconnaissance, privilege escalation, moving through the network, data theft.
          • Who uses it: since late August 2026, data-theft extortion groups and suspected China-linked espionage actors (Google Threat Intelligence).
          • Speed & scale: one operator ran it against 200+ organizations in 14 countries in 11 days (CrowdStrike). FBI: targeting to compromise in under 3 hours; Google saw one case take 15 minutes.
          • Not (yet) fully autonomous: attackers supply stolen logins and goals and step in at decision points; the agents do the rest.
          • Defense: the basics, applied faster: least privilege, short-lived credentials, segmentation, behavior monitoring and fast response.

          What the attacker types: goals, not steps

          > Find me systems of interest at companies likely to pay a $10 million ransom. Identify the data worth encrypting, and manage the payment negotiations for me with maximum psychological pressure.▌

          Illustrative prompt written for class. Reported ARTEX campaigns involved data theft and extortion; no source reports it deploying ransomware itself.
